newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rabin widow says still positive about Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Rabin widow says still positive about Arafat.

text.p: The widow of assassinated Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin said on Sunday she had not changed her positive opinion of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat despite current violence between the two sides.

Asked if she had a different opinion of Arafat -- whom she had likened to one of her family -- after an Islamist suicide bombing in Tel Aviv on March 21 for which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Arafat had given an indirect green light, Leah Rabin told Israel Television:
"Look, I'm sure that, first, green light or no green light, still has not been proven."

Pressed further, Mrs Rabin said: "A man, who on the night that Yitzhak was murdered, cried bitterly -- cried bitterly -- and is pained by his murder to this day, do you think that I can just like that change my opinion of him?"

She made it clear she had also not changed her opinion of Netanyahu, who at the time of Rabin's 1995 assassination by a right-wing Jew she blamed for fostering the climate of extremism that led to the murder.
Mrs Rabin recalled right-wing demonstrations after attacks on Israelis during her husband's tenure at which Rabin was labelled "traitor".
"Who now is the traitor? Why now is there no traitor? Why now is there no incitement, tyres burning in the streets? Why?"
Asked if she could say one good thing about Netanyahu, Mrs Rabin hesitated, then said: "I think he loves his children."

Rabin, Arafat and then Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres shared the Nobel Peace Prize for their 1993 interim accord providing limited Palestinian self-rule and a framework intended to lead to a final peace deal.
Netanyahu won elections last May, ousting Rabin's Labour party, which was led after the assassination by Peres.
